source.title: Emergent Symbolic Structure in Health Foundation Models: Extraction, Alignment, and Cross-Modal Transfer
source.authors: Gajendra J. Katuwal; Advait Koparkar; Salar Abbaspourazad; Anshuman Mishra; Sarvesh Kirthivasan

record.file_problem: none; the full paper, including supplementary material and Tables 4–6, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests cross-model representational alignment and transfer in health foundation models using post-hoc decomposition, matching, and CCA rather than the original studies’ methods or scale sweeps.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own cross-modal alignment, symbol-profile consistency, and transfer results. Cited claims and results from other work are not included. It does not vary model scale or capability.
record.test_reason: The study takes three independently trained wearable-health foundation models (PPG ViT, PPG EfficientNet, Accel ViT) and measures post-hoc linear alignment, cross-model transfer and the consistency of symbol health profiles. That is a new setting with its own results on V4, V5 and V6. There is no scale, quality or seed sweep.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that independently trained wearable health FMs share physiologically meaningful, linearly recoverable structure that supports cross-modal transfer from limited paired data. They read this as consistent with the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. They qualify it as empirical and dataset-specific, with no formal isomorphism claimed, and note the shared training population as a possible confound.
record.recipe_differences: Uses frozen health-sensor embeddings, linear decompositions, bijective matching and CCA, and downstream transfer/health-profile measures. It does not reproduce the original studies’ methods or test convergence over increasing scale.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment and transfer vary with extraction and alignment choices: ICA and NMF distribute bijective correspondence differently; CCA largely removes extractor differences; sparse-CCA regularization affects retained alignment; profile consistency also differs by extractor and model pair.

fits_no_version.finding: Extracted ICA components are selectively associated with specific health targets (Selectivity Index), while blood type stays uniformly low.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linearly decomposed foundation-model embeddings contain sparse, health-selective components.

record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, 2026 (as stated in the paper)
record.problems: All three models use the same ∼172K training population, so shared covariance is not separated from shared physiology; the authors identify disjoint-population comparisons as future evidence. The work uses linear decompositions and reports empirical rather than guaranteed alignment. Several detailed values are in figures and supplementary tables.
record.rows_left_out: The per-target transfer AUC and retention entries across alignment settings in Supplementary Tables 4–6 are not individually listed; the record includes the paper’s aggregate transfer results and its stated method comparisons (R13–R15, R18). The study reports many additional target-by-method cells.

untested.parts: No sweep over scale or capability.
There is no vision–language pairing, and model quality is not varied.
There is no comparison of the same architecture across seeds.

The causes of convergence (shared data or objective) are not isolated. All models share the same ~172K training population, and no disjoint-population comparison is made. A plateau with scale is not tested.
Stitching layers, relative representations and unpaired alignment are not tested.
Neuron, circuit and SAE feature identity are not tested; only the health profiles of linear components are.

missing.what: Per-method health-condition and physiological-marker transfer retention. Dense CCA gives about 85–90% (ICA, PCA) and about 69–81% (NMF), versus 94–99% for PCA+sparse CCA at λ=10⁻⁴. This shows the headline 98.7% is the best configuration.
Confounder baseline: every health condition's transfer AUC exceeds an age/sex/BMI-only baseline (no numbers in the text).
The selectivity results are robust when W1 is replaced by |Cohen's d|.

record.verdict_notes: The models are Apple health FMs: PPG ViT, PPG EfficientNet and Accel ViT, each producing 256-d embeddings. They share a training population, which the study cannot separate from shared physiology. The headline retention (more than 98%) is the best-case extractor/alignment combination; Tables 4–6 show lower retention for dense CCA and NMF. The text's claim that CCA makes extractors interchangeable (r≈0.99) does not carry over to transfer: PCA+dense CCA retains about 85–89% but PCA+sparse CCA about 98%. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep, and no comparison of independently trained models across increasing size or performance.
The study tests cross-modal alignment and transfer, but does not vary either model’s quality or performance to test whether alignment rises as both improve.
No different-seed comparison of networks with the same architecture.
Tests post-hoc linear alignment and transfer between health sensor models; does not test stitching layers, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
Tests recurrence of aligned, health-associated symbol profiles, not identity of neurons, circuits, or SAE features.
Tests sensitivity to extraction/alignment choices and sparse-CCA regularization. Does not compare a broad range of similarity metrics, neighbour settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
The study reports limits and notes that all models share a training population, but does not compare models trained on disjoint populations or isolate shared data/objectives as causes of alignment.

rows.subject: PPG EfficientNet vs Accel ViT
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-modal correspondence between raw embedding dimensions without alignment.
rows.note: The reported near-zero value applies to direct dimension-by-dimension comparison before alignment.
rows.check: Unaligned dimension-by-dimension correlation reflects basis mismatch, not absence of convergence. It shows the measure dependence V6 names: near zero raw, substantial once matched (R2). It has no bearing on V7.

source_check.locator_found: §4.1, paragraph comparing unaligned and bijectively aligned raw dimensions

rows.subject: PPG EfficientNet vs Accel ViT
rows.operation_detail: Applied bijective matching to raw embedding dimensions and measured their correspondence.
rows.measure: Head-10 correspondence and area under correlation curve
rows.baseline: Raw dimensions without alignment: near-zero cross-modal correlation
rows.value: Head-10 ≈ 0.56; area under the correlation curve ≈ 0.32
rows.note: Alignment recovers substantial correspondence, but this is not complete alignment.

rows.subject: PPG EfficientNet vs Accel ViT
rows.operation_detail: Compared bijectively matched cross-modal alignment across symbol extraction methods.
rows.measure: Area under the cross-modal correlation curve
rows.note: NMF alignment is more broadly distributed across symbols; ICA has stronger top-ranked matches but decays more rapidly.
rows.check: The extractor choice changes how bijective correspondence is distributed (AUC 0.39 vs 0.21). This is measure dependence, not evidence about the causes in V7, so V7 is removed.

rows.subject: PPG EfficientNet vs Accel ViT
rows.operation_detail: Aligned extracted symbols using CCA and measured cross-modal correlation.
rows.note: The paper notes that CCA maximizes cross-modal correlation and therefore largely bypasses the extractor’s basis.
rows.check: The state holds for V4. For V6 the extractor dependence is absent under CCA, since all extractors give near-identical curves. CCA maximises correlation by construction.

source_check.correct: V4: observed linear correspondence. V6: extractor dependence absent under dense CCA; ICA, PCA and NMF yield near-identical curves, with r ≈ 0.99 at top ranks.
source_check.problem: The single observed state incorrectly treats extractor dependence as observed for V6.

rows.subject: PPG EfficientNet vs Accel ViT
rows.operation_detail: Varied the L1 penalty in sparse CCA and measured retained alignment.
rows.measure: Alignment capacity relative to standard CCA
rows.note: The projections become sparser while retaining most, but not all, of standard CCA alignment.
rows.check: Keeping more than 95% of CCA capacity at λ ≤ 2×10⁻² counts as observed for V4, not partial.

source_check.correct: V4: observed. Within λ ≤ 2×10−2, the paper reports preserved alignment exceeding 95% of standard CCA; substantial setting dependence is established at high λ in R6, not by this condition alone.
source_check.problem: The observed state fits V4 but does not independently establish V6 within the stated regularization range.

rows.subject: PPG EfficientNet vs Accel ViT
rows.operation_detail: Varied the L1 penalty in sparse CCA and measured alignment degradation at higher sparsity.
rows.note: The text does not give a numeric alignment value for this condition.
rows.check: Alignment degrades at high λ, which is a setting dependence (V6). No number is given. It does not bear on V4.

source_check.locator_found: §4.1, sparse CCA paragraph spanning the page break

rows.subject: PPG ViT vs Accel ViT
rows.operation_detail: Compared the cosine similarity of cross-modal symbol W1 target profiles before and after ICA extraction and bijective alignment.
rows.measure: Median cosine similarity between cross-modal W1 target profiles; share of symbols above cosine 0.8
rows.value: ICA: median cosine 0.89; 91% of symbols above cosine 0.8
rows.note: The authors describe the aligned symbol profiles as having similar health associations across modalities.

rows.subject: Three model pairs: PPG ViT vs PPG EfficientNet; PPG ViT vs Accel ViT; PPG EfficientNet vs Accel ViT
rows.operation_detail: Compared median cosine similarity of symbol W1 target profiles across model pairs and extractors.
rows.uncertainty: Interquartile ranges shown in Figure 6; no numeric ranges stated in text
rows.note: The paper describes PCA profile similarity as architecture-invariant across these pairs.

source_check.correct: V5: observed profile consistency. V6: pair dependence absent for PCA in these comparisons; median profile cosine remains 0.90–0.91 across all pairs.
source_check.problem: The observed state fits V5, whereas the reported PCA result establishes robustness rather than V6 dependence.

rows.subject: Three model pairs: PPG ViT vs PPG EfficientNet; PPG ViT vs Accel ViT; PPG EfficientNet vs Accel ViT
rows.operation_detail: Compared median cosine similarity of symbol W1 target profiles across model pairs using ICA.

conditions.value: modality and architecture both differ in the most different pair

rows.baseline: ICA reaches 0.91 for the more similar pair
rows.value: Drops to 0.87 when both modality and architecture differ
rows.uncertainty: Interquartile ranges shown in Figure 6; no numeric ranges stated in text
rows.note: The authors attribute the lower ICA consistency to sensitivity of higher-order statistics to architectural nonlinearities.
rows.check: For V5 a median of 0.87 is still high consistency, only slightly lower. For V6 it shows extractor-by-pair dependence.

source_check.correct: V5: observed high profile consistency, with median cosine 0.87 for the pair differing in modality and architecture. V6: observed extractor-by-pair dependence, with ICA decreasing from 0.91 to 0.87.
source_check.problem: A decrease of 0.04 leaves high consistency and does not justify treating recurrence as clearly partial.

rows.subject: Three model pairs: PPG ViT vs PPG EfficientNet; PPG ViT vs Accel ViT; PPG EfficientNet vs Accel ViT
rows.operation_detail: Measured median cosine similarity of raw-embedding W1 target profiles across model pairs.
rows.uncertainty: Interquartile ranges shown in Figure 6; no numeric ranges stated in text
rows.note: The paper says extraction adds disentanglement and sharpens the alignment.
rows.check: A median cosine of 0.85 on raw embeddings already shows shared health profiles. That is observed for V5, not partial.

rows.subject: All three health foundation models; aggregate reported across models
rows.operation_detail: Transferred predictions between raw embeddings without symbol extraction or alignment.
rows.note: This is the raw-embedding transfer baseline.
rows.check: Transfer with no mapping at all cannot test whether a mapping exists. This is a trivial comparator.

rows.subject: All three health foundation models; aggregate across six directed domain pairs
rows.operation_detail: Transferred a classifier after bijective matching of raw embeddings.
rows.note: The paper says this remains well below CCA-based transfer.
rows.check: Tables 4–6 show Embed+Bijective health retention of 78–92%. V7 is removed because this row is about the mapping method, not the causes of convergence.

source_check.locator_found: §4.3, raw-transfer comparison; Figure 4a; Tables 4–6, Embed+Bijective column

rows.subject: All three health foundation models; aggregate across six directed domain pairs
rows.operation_detail: Trained a source-domain classifier and tested it on target-domain symbols after CCA-family alignment.
rows.measure: Transfer AUC and retention relative to in-domain AUC
rows.note: Aggregate result reported for health conditions; the supplementary tables give per-target and per-method values.
rows.check: 98.7% is the best configuration (PCA with sparse CCA at λ=10⁻⁴, 94–99%). Dense CCA gives about 85–90% (ICA, PCA) and 69–81% (NMF) per Tables 4–6. The CCA-family aggregate is selective. V7 is removed.

source_check.correct: §4.3 reports best transfer summaries of AUC 0.71–0.83 and retention 98.7% ± 1.6%. Restrict the condition to best-performing CCA-family configurations. §7.9 identifies PCA with sparse CCA, λ ≤ 10−3, as best across most targets; dense CCA is substantially worse in Tables 4–6.
source_check.problem: CCA family is too broad a condition for the selected near-lossless transfer summary.

rows.subject: All three health foundation models; aggregate reported across model pairs
rows.operation_detail: Transferred classifiers for physiological-marker targets after CCA-family alignment.
rows.measure: Transfer AUC and retention relative to in-domain AUC
rows.note: The text says physiological markers transfer most readily.
rows.check: About 100% retention holds only for PCA with sparse CCA. With dense CCA, PCA gives 83–85% (e.g. sex 0.83) and NMF 63–75% (Tables 5–6). V7 is removed.

source_check.correct: §4.3 reports physiological-marker AUC 0.88–1.00 and approximately 100% retention for best transfer. Restrict the condition to best-performing configurations; Table 5 supports near-total retention with PCA and weak sparse-CCA regularization, while dense CCA retains substantially less.
source_check.problem: Approximately 100% retention does not characterize the CCA family generally.

rows.subject: All three health foundation models; aggregate reported across six directed domain pairs
rows.operation_detail: Transferred classifiers for negative-control blood-type targets after alignment.
rows.baseline: In-domain AUC: target-dependent; chance level not stated numerically
rows.note: The study expects no meaningful blood-type transfer; this control does not measure whether meaningful target information maps across models.
rows.check: This is a negative control (blood type), not a measure of convergence.

rows.subject: All three health foundation models; aggregate across all targets and domain pairs
rows.operation_detail: Compared forward and reverse transfer after alignment.
rows.measure: Correlation between forward and reverse transfer AUC; mean absolute AUC difference
rows.note: The text reports similar retention in both transfer directions.

rows.subject: All three health foundation models; aggregate across eight health conditions
rows.operation_detail: Varied the fraction of paired subjects used to fit the alignment and measured transfer retention.
rows.value: All eight health conditions plateau above 95% retention by ∼7.5K paired subjects; further gains are marginal
rows.note: This is saturation with paired data for alignment, not a model-scale sweep.
rows.check: The map is estimated from about 30% of the paired cohort with retention above 95%, which supports a simple map. This is not a convergence plateau in the V7 sense.

rows.subject: All three health foundation models; aggregate reported across extraction and alignment methods
rows.operation_detail: Compared transfer outcomes across extraction and alignment methods.

conditions.value: bijective matching, sparse CCA, and dense CCA

rows.value: PCA with sparse CCA (λ ≤ 10−3) achieves the highest retention across most targets; NMF generally underperforms ICA and PCA; ICA with dense CCA is competitive but less robust across domain pairs
rows.note: The study reports that transfer outcomes depend on extraction/alignment choices. Tables 4–6 contain additional target-by-method values.
rows.check: Transfer clearly depends on extractor and alignment choices (NMF consistently lower, PCA+sparse CCA best). The numeric spread sits in Tables 4–6 but is not captured in the row.

source_check.correct: V6: observed extraction/alignment dependence. V4: observed near-lossless transfer for best PCA+sparse-CCA configurations, partial transfer for poorer configurations; split states by method.
source_check.problem: A single observed state masks the mixed V4 outcomes across the listed methods.

relationships.condition: Independently trained PPG/accelerometer health FMs, best linear (CCA-family) alignment
relationships.reason: Source classifiers retain about 98–100% of in-domain AUC (R13, R14). Retention is symmetric across directions (R16). The map is learned from about 30% of the pairs (R17). CCA correlation is about 0.99 (R4) and sparse CCA keeps more than 95% (R5).
relationships.display_finding: Classifiers retained about 98–100% of in-domain AUC symmetrically using maps learned from about 30% of pairs, with CCA correlation about 0.99 and sparse CCA retaining over 95%.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Independently trained PPG/accelerometer health FMs, best linear (CCA-family) alignment
source_check.reason: Best configurations preserve nearly all source AUC with linear alignment; symmetry and paired-data saturation provide additional evidence within this setting.

relationships.condition: Bijective matching, dense CCA, or NMF extraction rather than PCA+sparse CCA
relationships.reason: Raw bijective matching gives health mean AUC 0.67 (R12). Per Tables 4–6, dense CCA retains only about 85–90% for health conditions, and NMF is lower (R18). Near-lossless transfer therefore depends on the method choice.
relationships.display_finding: Raw bijective matching yielded mean health AUC 0.67, dense CCA retained about 85–90% for health conditions, and NMF performed worse than PCA with sparse CCA.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Bijective matching, dense CCA, or NMF extraction rather than PCA+sparse CCA
source_check.reason: R12 and Tables 4–6 show substantially reduced retention for these configurations, qualifying near-lossless interchangeability.

relationships.condition: W1 health-profile consistency of matched components across three model pairs
relationships.reason: The ICA median cosine is 0.89, with 91% of components above 0.8 (R7). PCA gives 0.90–0.91 across all pairs (R8). Raw embeddings already give 0.85 (R10).
relationships.display_finding: ICA achieved median cosine 0.89 with 91% of components above 0.8, while PCA reached 0.90–0.91 and raw embeddings reached 0.85.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: W1 health-profile consistency of matched components across three model pairs
source_check.reason: Matched components have strongly similar health profiles across models, supporting recurring task-related features without establishing neuron or circuit identity.

relationships.condition: ICA extraction when both modality and architecture differ
relationships.reason: The ICA median cosine drops from 0.91 to 0.87 for the most different pair (R9).
relationships.display_finding: Median ICA cosine similarity decreased from 0.91 to 0.87 for the most different model pair.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: ICA extraction when both modality and architecture differ
source_check.reason: Median cosine 0.87 remains high; the decrease from 0.91 establishes pair sensitivity but does not demonstrate failure or clearly incomplete recurrence in this condition.

relationships.condition: Unaligned vs matched comparison, bijective matching across extractors, sparse-CCA penalty, transfer across extractor/alignment
relationships.reason: Correlation is near zero unaligned but substantial matched (R1). The area under the curve varies with the extractor, 0.39 vs 0.21 (R3). Alignment degrades at high λ (R6). Profile consistency varies with extractor and pair (R9). Transfer retention varies strongly with the method (R18).
relationships.display_finding: Matching raised correlations from near zero to substantial values; extractor choice changed area under the curve from 0.39 to 0.21; high λ degraded alignment; profile consistency varied with extractor and model pair, while transfer retention varied with alignment method.

source_check.reason: Raw versus matched correlations, NMF versus ICA curve areas, high-penalty degradation and method-dependent transfer demonstrate protocol dependence.

relationships.reason: Under CCA the extractor choice barely matters: all extractors reach r ≈ 0.99 (R4). The measured alignment is robust to the basis there.
relationships.display_finding: All extractors reached approximately r=0.99, with little variation across bases.
